amendments.rule: An English particle or adverb that realizes a Greek **preverb** rides inside the compound verb's own unit and is never `added`, as a discontinuous realization under rule 15 where the ASV separates them: `ἐξῆλθεν` → *went forth*, `ἐξέβαλον` → *cast out*, `ἀνέβη` → *went up*, `ἐπεβίβασαν` → *set thereon* at LUK.19.35, `προσηργάσατο` → *hath made more* at LUK.19.16, `ἀπολάβωσιν` → *receive again* at LUK.6.34. The head is the English word glossing the **verbal root**, never the particle. The corpus is unanimous: 963 units across 141 chapters carry such a particle and every one of them is `aligned`, none `added`, and the head stands on the verb word in all but one class. This is scoped to a particle **no other source token stands to answer to**. Where an expressed preposition does answer to it — because the particle is part of that preposition's own English gloss, as *out* is of `ἐκ` → *out of* — the whole English prepositional expression is the preposition's, headed on the prepositional word, and the compound verb keeps only its verb word: `ἔξελθε ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *come* and *out of*, `ἐξῆλθεν ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *came* and *out of*, as `εἰσελθὼν εἰς` → *entered* and *into* and `ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ` → *departed* and *from* do. Rule 36 is what decides that and says it in terms: an English preposition governing a prepositional phrase realizes the Greek preposition and not the verb it depends on, even where English idiom makes the verb phrasal, and a preposition is left `unrepresented` only where English realizes it nowhere at all — so do not leave such a preposition a bare *of* while the verb takes the *out*. That arm is scoped to where the ASV writes **one** English particle for the two, and the count of English words the ASV wrote is what decides it, as rule 94 decides a compound unit by that same test. Where the ASV writes a particle for the preverb **in addition to** a complete prepositional expression, each token takes its own and the verb does not go bare: `Ἔξελθε … ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου` → *Come forth* and *out of the man* gives *forth* to the imperative and *out of* to `ἐκ`, as `τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν` → *the power proceeding from him had gone forth* gives *forth* to the participle and *proceeding from* to `ἐξ`. That the preverb and the preposition are the same morpheme is not the test and does not strand the extra word: this rule's own count forbids marking such a particle `added`, and rule 36 forbids handing it to a preposition whose English is already complete, so the verb is the only token left to take it. A **noncompositional prepositional phrase** standing in the same clause answers to the particle in the same way, and the single English word is that phrase's rather than the preverb's: `συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό` → *were gathered together* gives *were gathered* to the verb and *together* to `ἐπί` + `αὐτό` as one `noncompositional` unit under rule 45, the intervening article standing `unrepresented` under rule 93, as MAT.22.34 and ACT.4.26 read it and as ACT.2.44 reads the same phrase where no compound verb competes. Where no such phrase stands, the preverb keeps the word in the ordinary way, which is why `συνηγμένοι` → *gathered together* and `συνήχθησαν` → *were gathered together* keep *together* inside the verb's own unit. A preverb whose sense the following preposition's gloss does **not** carry keeps this rule's ordinary treatment, which is why `ἀναβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος` → *coming up out of the water* gives *up* to the participle and *out of* to `ἐκ` in one clause, and why `ἐκβάλλει … εἰς` → *driveth … forth* and *into* does. Rule 94 decides only whether the preposition and the word it governs form one unit, and does not decide where the particle goes. Where the compound verb governs a bare dative or genitive that the ASV writes with an English preposition, that preposition realizes the case government and rides with the governed word under rules 21, 36 and 69, as MRK.14.65 has it and as ACT.4.1 `ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς` → *came* and *upon them* and ACT.4.3 `ἐπέβαλον … αὐτοῖς` → *laid* and *on them* do. That arm too is scoped to where the ASV writes an English **verb word of its own** for the compound, as *came* and *laid* are. Where it writes none, and the English preposition is the only word carrying the compound's lexical sense, the preposition stays inside the verb's unit and the governed word takes its bare pronoun or noun: `προϊσταμένους ὑμῶν` → *are over* and *you* gives *are over* to the participle headed on *over* and a bare *you* to the genitive, `προΐστημι` meaning to stand before while *are* is only the periphrastic copula. Rule 17 is what forces this, forbidding a head on a subject or an auxiliary: a unit stripped to *are* would have no lexical word left to head on, whereas the governed word loses nothing, its case being what the verb's own sense already expresses. 1TH.5 writes both arms, giving *upon them* to the dative of `ἐφίσταται` → *cometh upon them* and keeping *over* with the participle of `προϊσταμένους`, which is what shows that an English verb word standing for the compound, and not which oblique case the verb governs, is what decides between those two. An **accusative** object is the contrast, and there the case is exactly what decides: English writes no preposition to realize an accusative, so where the ASV gives such an object an English preposition that preposition is the verb's own phrasal government and stays inside the verb's unit, the governed word keeping a bare noun or pronoun. `ἐκδεχομένου αὐτούς` → *waited for them* gives *waited for* to the participle and a bare *them* to the pronoun, as `ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτόν` → *feel after him* gives *feel after* to the optative and `ἀκούσαντες ἀνάστασιν` → *heard of the resurrection* gives *heard of* to the participle. Rules 21 and 36 are why: rule 21 hands a governed word the English preposition that realizes its **case**, and an accusative has none to realize, while rule 36 leaves a preposition with the verb only where no Greek preposition is expressed for it to answer to, which is exactly this configuration. ACT.17 writes both arms, giving *with them*, *with Paul*, *of him* and *unto him* to the oblique objects of `διαλέγομαι`, `προσκληρόομαι`, `ἐπιλαμβάνομαι` and `κολλάομαι` and keeping *for*, *after* and *of* inside the verbs of `ἐκδέχομαι`, `ψηλαφάω` and `ἀκούω`. Where a Greek preposition **is** expressed the question does not arise and rule 36 gives it the English word, as it does for `ἀκούω` with `περί` → *hear of your state*. So do not read a phrasal English verb as evidence that its particle belongs to the object: the test is whether the object's own case is a case English realizes with a preposition. The one exception is an idiom that leaves no English verb word to head on at all: `Ἆρον` → *away with him* at JHN.19.15 and `Αἶρε` → *away with* at LUK.23.18 head on *away*, because nothing else was written.
amendments.why: Rule 106's government arm named only a bare dative or genitive and so gave no answer for a compound verb governing a bare accusative whose object the ASV writes with an English preposition. ACT.17 supplies both arms in one chapter and separates them cleanly by case: the oblique objects of διαλέγομαι (17:2), προσκληρόομαι (17:4), ἐπιλαμβάνομαι (17:19) and κολλάομαι (17:34) carry 'with them', 'with Paul', 'of him' and 'unto him', while the accusative objects of ἐκδέχομαι (17:16), ψηλαφάω (17:27) and ἀκούω (17:32) stand bare and the verb keeps 'for', 'after' and 'of'. The reason is already in the contract: rule 21 gives a governed word the preposition that realizes its case, and an accusative has no case for a preposition to realize, so the word is the English verb's own phrasal government and rule 36 leaves it there, no Greek preposition being expressed to answer to it. I have added that clause and, so that the rule does not contradict itself, narrowed one existing sentence from 'not the case the verb governs' to 'not which oblique case the verb governs, is what decides between those two' — that sentence was distinguishing the two arms inside the oblique case, as its 1TH.5 evidence shows, and reads as a general denial only by accident. Nothing else in the rule is altered; every existing example, count and cross-reference is preserved verbatim.

conventions: Ἄρειος Πάγος is one aligned unit for the single English 'Areopagus', headed on Πάγος, and the governing article keeps its own 'the' (ACT.17.19 τὸν Ἄρειον Πάγον → 'the Areopagus', ACT.17.22 τοῦ Ἀρείου Πάγου → 'of the Areopagus'). Rule 94's test decides it: the ASV writes one English word for the two Greek tokens, and rule 35 keeps the unit aligned because '-pagus' answers to Πάγος and 'Areo-' to Ἄρειος.

πολιτάρχης → 'rulers of the city' is one aligned unit headed on 'rulers' (ACT.17.6, ACT.17.8). The -άρχης element is what that word glosses and 'of the city' is the supplied completion, so rule 66 heads it as ἀρχιερεύς → 'chief priest' heads on 'priest'. No token of the verse answers to 'city' separately.

ἕως governing a genitive and rendered by the frame 'as far as' takes all three English words as one unit headed on 'far' (ACT.17.14, ACT.17.15). At 17:14 the following ἐπί keeps its own 'to' and the article its own 'the', so the frame does not reach across into the governed phrase.

A supplied adversative juncture is placed exactly as rule 88 places a supplied 'and': at ACT.17.30 the 'but' introducing the main clause after the converted circumstantial participle ὑπεριδών is a rule 7 helper on παραγγέλλει, the finite verb it introduces. It is not `added` under rule 86, a participle standing in the clause being a licensing token, and it does not go to the article of the adverbial τὰ νῦν, which contributes no part of the English 'now' (rule 93). Rule 88's own wording names only 'and', so a later chapter meeting another adversative should say in the note that this reading rests on ACT.17.30.

The θέλω idiom is decided by the count of English words the ASV wrote, not by the Greek. θέλει … εἶναι → 'mean' at ACT.17.20 is one `noncompositional` unit, no part of that word answering to either lexeme (rules 45, 73). ἂν θέλοι … λέγειν → 'would … say' at ACT.17.18 splits instead: λέγειν keeps 'say' and ἄν with θέλοι takes 'would' as one `aligned` unit, so that rule 50 leaves the particle nowhere empty. Giving 'would' to ἄν alone and leaving θέλοι unrepresented remains defensible and is named in that unit's note.

report: Read all 34 verses end to end against the 65-lemma candidate table. No construction is analysed two ways without a source or ASV-phrasing difference licensing it, so no patches.

τε and μέν are uniform under rule 70: a connective τε with no answering καί keeps its own conjunction (17:4 twice, 17:19, 17:26), the τε of a τε…καί pair with one written conjunction is empty (17:10, 17:14), and μέν is empty in all four instances (17:12, 17:17, 17:30, 17:32). 17:14 writes both τε shapes in one verse and treats each correctly.

Article handling checked across all 98 occurrences. Article-before-a-name is empty throughout; ὁ θεός takes 'The' at 17:24 and nothing at 17:30 because the ASV writes the determiner in one and not the other (rules 19, 23). The possessive chain is rule 76's own contrast: the article is empty wherever a free genitive pronoun stands (17:16, 17:20, 17:26, 17:28) and takes 'his' only at 17:2, where Παύλῳ has been spent on the English subject.

πάντα / τὰ πάντα / κατὰ πάντα looked like a three-way split and is not: at 17:24 the article governs ἐν αὐτῷ and is emptied by the fused 'therein' (rule 93), at 17:25 it governs the quantifier and takes the supplied 'things' (rule 102), at 17:22 the Greek is anarthrous and 'things' is a rule 7 helper on the quantifier (rule 17).

The postposed τῶν of 17:4 is empty while the preposed τῶν of the same verse takes 'of the'. That is rule 31's placement test as rule 57 routes it, and 17:12's postposed τῶν εὐσχημόνων agrees; the second attributive articles of 17:19 and 17:24 are empty on the same rule.

Read the ASV italics by hand, the candidate table being blind to added units. Supplied 'one' (17:7) and 'their' (17:26) fold onto the anarthrous word they determine under rules 11 and 51; supplied 'said he' (17:3) is added because no verb of speaking stands in the verse and ὅτι is already spent on 'that'. Determiner folds against an unlicensed lexical verb are different tests, consistently applied.

The one general finding: compound verbs governing a bare case split cleanly by case, and the split is invisible from inside any one verse. διαλέγομαι, προσκληρόομαι, ἐπιλαμβάνομαι and κολλάομαι put 'with them', 'with Paul', 'of him' and 'unto him' on the oblique object (17:2, 17:4, 17:19, 17:34), while ἐκδέχομαι, ψηλαφάω and ἀκούω keep 'for', 'after' and 'of' inside the verb and leave the accusative object bare (17:16, 17:27, 17:32). Rule 106 names only a bare dative or genitive, so I have amended it rather than adding a cross-referencing rule.

BSB: all thirteen disagreements are documented convention differences or readings whose competing analysis the verse note already names — rule 70 (μέν 17:30), rule 93 (τό 17:11), rule 31 (ὁ 17:24), rule 36 (καθ 17:28, κατά 17:17), rules 21/23 (τῶν 17:28, τῆς 17:30), rule 38 (Οἱ 17:6), rule 67 (ὡς 17:15). καί at 17:5 is correct: the ASV writes one 'and' in that stretch and it answers to the καί before ὀχλοποιήσαντες. None is a genuine error, and nothing was changed to move the aggregate.

Not promoted, deliberately: the supplied adversative juncture 'but' at 17:30 extends rule 88's 'and' on a single instance with no corpus precedent shown, so it is recorded as a convention instead. If later chapters accumulate more, it belongs in rule 88's text.
